video.title: I Make $13K/Month From (Yet Another) Fitness App

summary: Max describes building Max AI, a mobile lifting and fitness app, after noticing that lifters used several separate apps without one unified platform. He had little coding experience and used AI coding tools, then charged an upfront annual fee and grew through founder-led social content and paid ads. He says the app brought in nearly $14,000 over the prior 28 days, with growth from X, app downloads, and subscribers. His main advice is to launch around a problem you care about, learn which features and videos work, and share the building process publicly.

ideas.name: Max AI fitness app
ideas.one_liner: A mobile fitness app combining lifting logs, tailored workout programs, nutrition, sleep, supplement tracking, and an AI coach.
ideas.business_model: Upfront annual app fee; the founder says it is charged yearly rather than relying on users to forget to cancel.
ideas.customer: People who lift and want a unified health and fitness app; the founder says he and his college friends lifted and that users seek a lifting app.
ideas.problem: Lifters were using different apps, without one unified platform for training and related health tracking.
ideas.offer: A mobile app with workout scheduling and tracking, nutrition and supplement and peptide tracking, sleep information, workout tutorials, saved templates, a leaderboard, a social feed, and a chat coach that adjusts workouts and can create recipes.

pricing.model: Upfront yearly fee for the app; renewal terms beyond the stated yearly charge are not explained.
pricing.notes: The founder says the app was not intended to rely on users forgetting to cancel a subscription.

acquisition_channels.details: Max filmed his own short videos daily, studied their hold and skip rates, and used founder-led content to share his journey. He also tweeted about the business on X; he says people following him there contributed roughly a third of revenue. He says clipping has brought international exposure and organic downloads.

quote.text: So I started filming every day, five videos, 10 videos, getting over kind of that initial cringe and fear of your friend sending you around and laughing at you.
quote.speaker: Max

acquisition_channels.details: He ran better-performing videos as paid ads, started with a low budget, and raised spend as he saw product-market fit. He says Meta performed better than TikTok for his app and that views there had higher intent and willingness to pay.

quote.text: I started on a low budget at first. But as I started to see that there really was product market fit. I started to still be up to budget and now we're spending around $250 a day on paid ads.
quote.speaker: Max

acquisition_channels.details: He planned a campaign to recruit five other people to make videos every day. The transcript does not identify the campaign platform.

quote.text: And finally, starting a side shift campaign to get, you know, five other people like me that can make videos every single day as well.
quote.speaker: Max

ideas.delivery: The app is delivered on iOS. Users access tracking, workout schedules, saved templates, leaderboards, a social feed, and an AI chat coach in the app. Max says the coach can adjust workouts and generate a recipe from ingredients the user has. The founder builds and updates the software; the transcript does not describe customer support or a human coaching service.
unit_economics_claims: Max says the app generated nearly USD 14,000 in revenue over the prior 28 days.
Max describes monthly revenue as roughly USD 14,000 to USD 15,000.
Max says he charged USD 24.99 upfront for a yearly fee, which he described as about USD 2 per month.
Max reports 1,000 active subscribers, more than 20,000 new customers in 28 days, more than 40,000 all-time, and 20,000 iOS downloads.
Max says paid ads were costing around USD 250 per day.
Max says roughly one-third of revenue came from people on X.
Max says Supabase cost USD 20 per month; he does not give a total operating cost.
ideas.startup_cost: Total startup cost not stated. Max describes the stack as inexpensive, mentions a USD 15 Claude Code membership and Supabase at USD 20 per month, and gives no prices for Vercel, Expo, or RevenueCat.
ideas.time_to_first_revenue: Not stated as an interval from launch. Max says he got his first paying customer four months before the interview and describes building the app over roughly six months.

acquisition.how: Agents could help draft, edit, clip, schedule, and analyze social posts and manage ad reporting. A founder or creator still needs to provide credible fitness content and approve claims and creative; Max’s approach depended on filming himself.

onboarding.how: App sign-up and collection of user preferences could be handled in software, with occasional review of onboarding problems. The transcript does not describe the actual onboarding flow.

delivery.how: The app automates tracking and the coach can adjust workout plans and produce recipes. Human review remains useful for potentially unsafe training, nutrition, supplement, or peptide guidance.

billing.how: App Store and RevenueCat can handle payments and access to the paid app. The transcript does not explain renewals, refunds, or billing support.

support.how: Automated help could answer routine app questions, but fitness and health-related questions may need human review. The founder does not describe a support process.

uk_applicability.notes: Lifting, workout tracking, and mobile fitness apps can serve UK users. Pricing, privacy handling for health-related data, and safety review for nutrition and supplement features would need suitable UK localisation.

risks: The founder acknowledges a crowded market, including many existing lifting apps.
Growth depends partly on founder-led content and paid social ads; ad costs or platform performance could change.
Workout, nutrition, sleep, supplement, and peptide features can create user-safety and privacy risks. The transcript does not describe safeguards or clinical review.
The founder says he is reinvesting earnings into growth, but gives no profit, retention, refund, or customer acquisition cost figures.

tactics.name: Find a familiar problem in a fragmented category
steps: Start with a category you care about and already use.
Ask whether customers are using several separate apps for one job.
Build a unified product if the gap is meaningful, even if competitors already exist.

quote.text: There were a few different apps that people were using. There wasn't really one unified platform, so I just went out and built it.
quote.speaker: Max

tactics.name: Charge for the app instead of relying on forgotten cancellations
steps: Set an upfront yearly fee.
Explain the annual charge as a simple monthly equivalent.
Max says this avoids depending on users forgetting to cancel.

quote.text: So we just charged an upfront $24.99 a yearly fee, which is just really $2 a month.
quote.speaker: Max

tactics.name: Use founder-made videos to test creative
steps: Film several short videos every day rather than paying creators before the product and message are clear.
Track hold rate and skip rate for each video.
Use the strongest formats as the basis for further promotion.

quote.text: I was looking at all of the videos I posted and analyzed what's the hold rate? What's the skip rate? And then I started running the best performers as paid ads.
quote.speaker: Max

tactics.name: Scale ad spend after signs of product-market fit
steps: Start paid promotion with a low budget.
Watch for evidence that the product and creative are working.
Increase spend once performance supports it; Max reported spending around USD 250 a day at the time of the interview.

quote.text: I started on a low budget at first. But as I started to see that there really was product market fit. I started to still be up to budget and now we're spending around $250 a day on paid ads.
quote.speaker: Max

tactics.name: Delay hiring UGC creators until the message is clear
steps: First define the app's scope and learn which features drive downloads.
Identify the angles and formats that work.
Only then consider paying UGC creators, to avoid burning money on unproven creative.

quote.text: I would say we don't really have the scope defined of your app yet. And you don't understand what features are going to drive downloads. It's very early on, I would avoid hiring UGC creators.
quote.speaker: Max

tactics.name: Prioritise Meta over TikTok based on the app’s results
steps: Compare paid results across platforms instead of assuming they perform alike.
For this app, Max preferred Meta because he believed its views were more valuable and its buyers had higher intent and willingness to pay.

quote.text: I would say right now, met as much better than TikTok. I think the views are more valuable. I think they're higher intent buyers.
quote.speaker: Max

tactics.name: Share the founder journey publicly
steps: Post progress and lessons on X consistently.
Share what is working, what is not, and vulnerabilities rather than hiding the business.
Use founder-led content to help prospective customers follow the product's development.

quote.text: Be as public about it as possible. Show everyone what's working, what's not. Tell them about your vulnerabilities. People are really supportive.
quote.speaker: Max

tactics.name: Use clipping to widen organic reach
steps: Turn existing video material into clips for broader distribution.
Max says clipping can bring international exposure and organic app downloads.

quote.text: This is a great way to get international exposure and a great way to get organic downloads.
quote.speaker: Max

lessons.lesson: A crowded market can still have room for a product that makes a fragmented user experience feel unified.

quote.text: There were a few different apps that people were using. There wasn't really one unified platform, so I just went out and built it.

lessons.lesson: A founder’s personal brand and visible journey can help attract users and build support around a product.

quote.text: I think building your personal brand is one of the most powerful things you can do.
quote.speaker: Max

lessons.lesson: Use your own content to discover which messages work before hiring creators to repeat them.

quote.text: I was looking at all of the videos I posted and analyzed what's the hold rate? What's the skip rate?
quote.speaker: Max

lessons.lesson: Start paid marketing at a small scale and increase spending when there is evidence that the product and creative are working.

quote.text: I started on a low budget at first. But as I started to see that there really was product market fit.
quote.speaker: Max

lessons.lesson: Do not assume that an idea needs to be completely new; passion and a useful execution can matter in an established category.

quote.text: I wasn't naive to the fact that there were 100 other competitors already out there. But I wanted to build something I was actually passionate about.
quote.speaker: Max

lessons.lesson: Share what is working and what is not; Max says people can be supportive rather than simply copying the idea.

quote.text: Be as public about it as possible. Show everyone what's working, what's not. Tell them about your vulnerabilities. People are really supportive.

evidence_quality.rationale: The guest is the first-hand founder and gives specific product details, growth metrics, prices, tools, and marketing steps. The numbers are self-reported and the transcript provides little evidence about profit, retention, acquisition costs, or independent verification. The transcript is local Whisper output and contains apparent recognition errors, including software and platform names.
evidence_quality.promotional_conflict: The video includes a sponsored HubSpot CRM read. Max does not appear to sell a course or software in the interview.
